title: Moral relativism
examples: Does what is right in one country have to be right everywhere?
Can we judge another culture's morals?
Is there one set of rules for being good?

explain.say: Today we explore if right and wrong are the same everywhere.
Moral relativism suggests morality depends on culture or society.
For example, some cultures view certain clothing as inappropriate.
Another example is how different societies view personal space.

items: Step 1: Culture A: Close proximity accepted
Step 2: Culture B: More distance preferred

explain.say: In everyday life, think about greetings in different countries.

items: A hug in a third place

explain.say: A common mistake is assuming your own culture's rules are always best.

draw.text: Mistake: Assuming your culture is best

faq.q: If morality is relative, does that mean nothing can be truly wrong?
faq.a: It suggests that 'wrong' is defined by a specific group's standards. You might also ask: Does this mean we have no moral rules? Or: Is everything acceptable if culture decides it?
asks: Can we ever say something is wrong for everyone?

faq.q: How do we know what the 'correct' culture's rules are?
faq.a: We can only observe what different cultures believe at any given time. You might ask: Which culture has the best morals? Or: Is it impossible to judge any culture?
asks: How do we compare moral systems?
Is there a better way to judge ethics?

faq.q: Does moral relativism mean people can just do whatever they want?
faq.a: No, it means their actions are judged by their own group's rules. You might ask: Does this mean no rules apply? Or: Can I break rules if my group says it is okay?
asks: Are there any limits to freedom?

faq.q: What is the difference between cultural norms and moral truths?
faq.a: Cultural norms are habits or expected behaviors, while moral truths are beliefs about right and wrong. You might ask: Are they always connected? Or: Is a custom always a moral rule?
asks: Are customs the same as morals?
Can a habit be morally wrong?

faq.q: Does this idea apply to historical periods too?
faq.a: Yes, we can look at how past societies held different moral views. You might ask: Did people in the past think differently? Or: Does time change morality?
asks: How did past societies view ethics?
Was morality different in the past?

facts: Moral relativism suggests that moral judgments are relative to culture.
A universal morality suggests certain rules apply to all people everywhere.
Anthropology often studies how different cultures develop unique moral codes.
The concept forces us to consider the source of moral authority.

quiz.say: If a society believes stealing is acceptable for survival, a moral relativist would say:

options.show: C. It is only wrong if caught.
options.say: C. It is only wrong if caught.

options.show: D. It is only wrong for outsiders.
options.say: D. It is only wrong for outsiders.

options.show: B. It is right within that society's rules.
options.say: B. It is right within that society's rules.

quiz.why: This shows that the moral judgment depends on the society's accepted rules.

wrong.0: This assumes universal morality, ignoring the society's rules.
wrong.1: This focuses only on punishment, not the moral belief itself.
wrong.2: This is too extreme; it ignores the possibility of internal disagreement.

quiz.say: If you meet someone from a culture that practices a custom you find offensive, a moral relativist might suggest:
quiz.show: A. Judge it by your standards.

options.show: A. Judge it by your standards.
options.say: A. Judge it by your standards.

options.show: C. Tell them they must change.
options.say: C. Tell them they must change.

options.show: B. Understand it within their context.
options.say: B. Understand it within their context.

quiz.why: This approach requires understanding the culture's internal framework for morality.

wrong.0: This is ethnocentrism, judging others by your own culture.
wrong.1: This assumes your culture's way is the only correct way.
wrong.2: This avoids the discussion rather than understanding it.

quiz.say: Which statement best describes the core idea of moral relativism?
quiz.show: A. Morality is fixed by nature.

options.show: D. Morality is determined by personal feeling.
options.say: D. Morality is determined by personal feeling.

options.show: B. Morality is determined by culture or society.
options.say: B. Morality is determined by culture or society.

options.show: A. Morality is fixed by nature.
options.say: A. Morality is fixed by nature.

options.show: C. Morality is determined by the strongest group.
options.say: C. Morality is determined by the strongest group.

quiz.why: This captures the idea that moral standards are not fixed universally.

wrong.0: This is subjective egoism, which is often too narrow for cultural study.
wrong.2: This represents universalism, which is the opposite idea.
wrong.3: This suggests power dictates morality, which is a political view, not purely philosophical.
